1. Abstract  ![](data:image/png;base64,)

Natural disasters such as earthquakes frequently cause collapsed structures and highly unstructured terrains, posing severe risks to human rescuers. However, conventional mobile robots with a single locomotion mode struggle to simultaneously achieve the high-speed mobility required for rapid deployment and the terrain adaptability needed to traverse rubble and uneven surfaces. 

To address this challenge, this paper presents a transformable hexapod robot with hybrid track-legged locomotion, governed by a hierarchical three-mode control architecture. The robot integrates six 3-DOF track-legs on a hexagonal body, enabling switching between tracked and hexapod modes. A high-level mode selector switches among a walking mode based on impedance-controlled tripod gait for uneven terrain, a tracked mode using differential PID control for rapid traversal, and a climbing mode driven by a reinforcement learning agent that jointly coordinates leg joint torques and track velocities to surmount large vertical obstacles such as stairs. 

The integrated design enables seamless locomotion mode switching, with the reinforcement learning agent specifically trained to enable the robot to autonomously climb stairs, significantly enhancing overall adaptability in disaster rescue scenarios. 

1. Introduction ![](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAYAAAAXCAYAAAAoRj52AAAABHNCSVQICAgIfAhkiAAAAAlwSFlzAAAOxAAADsQBlSsOGwAAAE9JREFUKJHt0aERgDAQRNF/CYOmlJQQjb8qrxgqoQU2FuYySBRf7pMLbwnsaG27bwUg8EJd9wTugGQJZv3wCVQzZYjQJU7B4ywEpt6XBLMGPp0RKiaiMyEAAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

Natural disasters such as earthquakes, building collapses, and post-explosion incidents generate highly unstructured environments characterized by rubble, narrow passages, and discontinuous terrain features including stairs and debris piles. Deploying human rescuers in such scenarios carries significant risk of secondary injury, motivating the development of mobile robots capable of autonomous search-and-rescue (SAR) operations [1], [2]. Recent surveys highlight that the effectiveness of disaster-response robots is fundamentally constrained by their locomotion capabilities, particularly when navigating the discontinuous vertical obstacles commonly encountered in collapsed-structure scenarios [1], [3]. 

Mobile ground robots are conventionally categorized by their locomotion mechanism into wheeled, tracked, legged, and hybrid systems [4]. Wheeled robots offer high-

speed mobility and energy efficiency on flat surfaces but lack the terrain adaptability  ![ref1]required to surmount large obstacles. Tracked robots provide a larger ground contact  area suitable for soft or sloped terrain, yet their continuous chassis profile restricts  agility in confined spaces. Legged robots, particularly hexapods, exhibit superior  adaptability to complex environments owing to their statically stable gait patterns and  discrete ground contact [4], [5]. However, purely legged systems sacrifice locomotion  efficiency on flat surfaces and exhibit limited capability when negotiating large  vertical obstacles such as stairs. To address these complementary trade-offs, hybrid  locomotion systems integrating multiple modalities have attracted increasing research  attention in recent years.  

A variety of hybrid track-leg, wheel-leg, and wheel-track transformable robots have  recently been proposed to combine the speed of wheeled or tracked locomotion with  the obstacle-negotiation capability of legged systems. TALBOT [6] introduced a  quadruped track-leg transformable structure capable of switching between tracked and  legged modes via folding linkages, controlled by a CPG-based locomotion strategy.  The WheTLHLoc 4W [7] integrates two tracks, two rotating legs, and four wheels in  a compact body, with the track length explicitly designed to fit a single stair tread.  The α-WaLTR robot [8] employs four passively transformable wheels with embedded  spring suspension for multi-terrain locomotion, while the QuadRunner platform [9]  leverages a four-bar leg mechanism for body-shifted obstacle surmounting. Additional  designs such as the reconfigurable wheel-track robot in [10], the wheel-spoke-paddle  amphibious robot in [11], and the spherical wheel-legged hybrid in [12] further  illustrate the breadth of recent transformable concepts. Despite these advances, three  critical limitations persist across existing hybrid designs. Most prevailing  architectures—including TALBOT [6], WheTLHLoc 4W [7], and QuadRunner [9]— are quadruped-dominant, limiting their static stability margins on irregular terrain  compared to hexapod alternatives [4], [5]. Their obstacle-climbing capability is also  restricted, with empirical studies reporting maximum climbable heights typically  below the robot's own body length—for example, approximately 22 cm for a wheel- legged hexapod [13] and a single stair tread for WheTLHLoc 4W [7]. Furthermore,  most existing designs treat track propulsion and leg articulation as two independent  control problems, lacking a unified framework that exploits the coupled dynamics of  tracks and legs during climbing tasks.  

To generate stable locomotion patterns for legged robots, the bio-inspired Central  Pattern Generator (CPG) has been widely adopted as a low-dimensional rhythmic  signal generator [5], [14]. CPG-based controllers have demonstrated capability in  producing tripod gaits, gait transitions, and local reactive behaviors such as elevator  and searching reflexes [5], [15]. However, three intrinsic limitations restrict the  ![ref1]applicability of CPG-based methods in non-structured rescue environments. Coupled- oscillator parameters such as natural frequency, coupling weights, and amplitude must  be hand-tuned or optimized offline via genetic algorithms or Bayesian optimization  [16], rendering rapid adaptation to unforeseen terrain infeasible. CPG-driven gaits  also exhibit reduced stability when traversing highly irregular surfaces, since the  open-loop oscillatory dynamics cannot directly encode high-dimensional terrain  features [14], [17]. Moreover, extending CPG to coordinate heterogeneous  actuators—such as legs and tracks simultaneously—requires hierarchical oscillator  networks whose parameter dimensionality grows rapidly with the number of coupled  limbs [15], [18]. These limitations motivate the recent shift toward learning-based  methods that can autonomously discover locomotion policies from data, without  relying on hand-designed oscillatory primitives.  

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for legged  locomotion, enabling policies that adapt to complex terrains without explicit  dynamics models [19]–[21]. Recent works have demonstrated DRL-based controllers  for quadruped stair climbing [22], wheeled-legged urban navigation [23], and  hexapod walking over uneven terrain [19]. Nevertheless, applying end-to-end DRL to  a multi-modal hybrid track-leg hexapod robot encounters three significant challenges.  Jointly learning track velocities and six-leg joint torques results in a high-dimensional  action space that drastically slows policy convergence and increases the risk of failure  modes during training [19], [21]. Purely end-to-end DRL policies also do not  naturally encode discrete behavioral transitions—such as walking, tracked, and  climbing modes—often producing oscillatory or ambiguous mode selection on the  boundary of operating regimes [24], [25]. In addition, unconstrained DRL exploration  may yield policies that violate physical safety constraints or produce uninterpretable  behaviors, posing significant risks for deployment in unstructured rescue scenarios  [25], [26]. These observations motivate the integration of DRL with rule-based  supervisory logic that explicitly encodes mode-switching priors, thereby reducing the  exploration burden and ensuring deterministic safety-critical behaviors.  

To address the aforementioned limitations, this work proposes a hierarchical control  framework that synergistically combines a Finite State Machine (FSM) supervisor  with mode-specific reinforcement learning policies. The high-level FSM monitors the  chassis pitch angle α and local terrain elevation Δh from onboard IMU and  exteroceptive scans, switching the execution mode M(t) deterministically among three  regimes: a walking mode M\_leg for moderately uneven terrain, a tracked mode  M\_track for flat open surfaces, and a climbing mode M\_climb when α or Δh exceeds  

predefined thresholds. In the walking mode, an RL policy generates the desired foot- ![ref1]tip trajectories in task space—replacing the conventional hand-tuned CPG  oscillators—and the trajectories are subsequently tracked by an operational-space  impedance controller [27], yielding compliant interaction with uneven terrain while  maintaining body posture stability. In the climbing mode, a decoupled hybrid strategy  is deployed in which an RL policy trained in NVIDIA Isaac Sim coordinates the six- leg joint angles to negotiate the irregular obstacle profile, while the dual-track linear  velocity is governed deterministically by FSM logic to provide persistent forward  thrust against the obstacle wall. In the tracked mode, a conventional differential PID  controller with IMU-based attitude compensation regulates the dual-track velocities,  ensuring cross-slope stabilization and precise path tracking. This RL + FSM  architecture preserves the adaptability of learning-based methods within each mode  while leveraging the structural clarity of rule-based supervisory logic to handle  discrete mode transitions, directly addressing the exploration-space, mode-switching,  and safety limitations of end-to-end DRL.  

The main contributions of this work are as follows. First, this paper presents a  transformable hexapod robot featuring a novel **asymmetric track-leg configuration**  in which the four outer legs (two front and two rear) integrate miniature track modules  driven by overhead DC motors at their distal ends, while the two middle legs remain  as pure articulated legs. This design exploits the four corner track-legs for high-speed  continuous propulsion in tracked mode, while preserving the agility and stability  functions of the middle legs—particularly for foot placement on irregular terrain and  active stance adjustment during climbing. The proposed robot is capable of climbing  obstacles up to **XX times its body length**, substantially exceeding the climbing  capability of existing hybrid track-leg robots.  

Second, a reinforcement learning–based trajectory generator is developed to replace  conventional CPG oscillators in the walking mode. The proposed RL policy achieves  **XX% higher average walking speed** and **XX% lower body pitch/roll variance**  compared with CPG-based and end-to-end DRL baselines, while requiring **XX%  fewer training episodes** to reach convergence—demonstrating that the proposed  framework produces a more efficient and stable walking gait than prior learning- based approaches.  

Third, an RL + FSM hierarchical control framework is proposed to directly resolve  the inherent coupling between track and leg dynamics during climbing tasks. Because  analytical decoupling of the coupled track-leg system is intractable, the proposed  framework trains a reinforcement learning agent end-to-end within the climbing mode  

while the finite state machine supervises high-level mode transitions, providing ![](data:image/png;base64,)structural priors that compress the RL exploration space and guarantee safety-critical behaviors. 

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the mechanical design and hardware specifications of the proposed robot. Section III presents the hierarchical RL + FSM control architecture in detail. Section IV reports the Isaac Sim simulation experiments and performance evaluation. Section V concludes the paper and discusses future directions. 

2. Robot Design ![](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAQAAAAYCAYAAADd5VyeAAAABHNCSVQICAgIfAhkiAAAAAlwSFlzAAAOxAAADsQBlSsOGwAAAEpJREFUGJXl0LENgCAURdEDRHdwDlrXYEpWcQzXMN9GiYmNvbd6OeXjU1utS5Agw6ysvbU8AFO7RoYjInnCsx9CCbveY2iQ7k9fnaYRDZ+NSotTAAAAAElFTkSuQmCC)
1. **Mechanical Structure** 

The mechanical design of the proposed robot is inspired by two arthropod species exhibiting complementary locomotion capabilities. The arthropod spider serves as the primary bionic model owing to its exceptional stability and flexibility on irregular substrates [27], [28], and arthropod-inspired designs have been widely adopted in legged robotics for their inherent multi-DOF mobility and adaptability across complex terrains [28], [29]. Although spiders possess eight legs, only six are primarily used for locomotion while the front pair is dedicated to feeding and pushing obstacles [27]; this observation justifies the six-legged simplification adopted in this work, which reduces structural complexity, weight, and control bandwidth requirements while retaining the spider's agile climbing characteristics. Inspired by this anatomy, the robot adopts a hexagonal body as its core frame, providing high structural symmetry and expandability, with six legs symmetrically mounted around the body, as shown in Fig. 1. 

While hexapod robots inherit the climbing agility of arthropod spiders, their cyclic stepping motion intrinsically limits average forward speed on flat, open terrain. To address this efficiency gap, the proposed robot draws additional inspiration from the water strider (Gerridae), whose mid-pair limbs perform rapid rowing strokes to achieve high-speed locomotion across the water surface—a hydrodynamic mechanism characterized in detail by Hu *et al.* [30] and subsequently transferred to multi-legged robotic platforms in [28]. However, the continuous flexibility and high degrees-of- freedom exhibited by living arthropods are intrinsically supported by hydrostatic

joints, deformable cuticles, and densely innervated muscles—properties that are  ![ref1]difficult to replicate in physical robots constrained by the discrete torque capacity,  finite axis count, and rigid structural materials of commercially available servo  actuators. The proposed design therefore does not pursue direct biomimetic  replication, but instead approximates the spider's static stability and the water strider's  continuous propulsion through a hardware-feasible asymmetric configuration: the four  outer legs are augmented with miniature track modules driven by overhead DC  motors at their distal ends, while the two middle legs remain as pure articulated limbs  to preserve agility for irregular foot placement and active stance adjustment.  

The key innovation of this design lies in the asymmetric track-leg mechanism  illustrated in Fig. 2. Unlike conventional hexapod legs that terminate in a passive foot  pad, the four outer legs (two front and two rear) of the proposed robot each integrate a  miniature track module at its distal end. This dual-function structure serves as an  articulated leg end-effector in hexapod mode and as a driven track unit in tracked  mode—all within the same mechanical assembly without requiring additional  actuators or reconfigurable parts. Each leg consists of three servo-driven joints: the  coxa joint for horizontal hip rotation, the femur joint for vertical hip swing, and the  tibia joint for knee flexion. In hexapod mode, all six legs coordinate to produce  precise swing, lift, and foot placement motions for traversal of irregular terrain. In  tracked mode, the joint servos maintain a fixed structural posture while JGB37-520  DC motors drive the four corner track modules, propelling the robot like a compact  tracked vehicle with high ground contact area for stability on soft or sloped surfaces;  the two middle legs simultaneously retract into the body envelope to minimize ground  interference.  

This unified track-leg structure significantly reduces mechanical complexity  compared to designs that use separate locomotion subsystems for each mode, thereby  lowering the risk of mechanical failure and simplifying the transformation process.  The mode transition, shown in Fig. 3, is accomplished by simultaneously  commanding all six leg joints to retract from walking posture into a low-profile  tracked configuration, completing the transformation in approximately 9.5 seconds.  The robot dimensions are 500 mm × 500 mm × 350 mm in hexapod mode and 600  mm × 400 mm × 300 mm in tracked mode.  

B. Hardware Specification  

The system hardware architecture is shown in Fig. 4, and full specifications are  summarized in Table I. The main computing unit is an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano,  

responsible for AI inference, motion control command generation, and sensor data ![](data:image/png;base64,)integration. Leg actuation is provided by HTD-45H servo motors coordinated through a Hiwonder Bus Servo Controller, while track propulsion is driven by JGB37-520 DC motors controlled via an Arduino L293D motor driver. The sensor suite includes a RealSense D415 depth camera for environment perception and object detection, a SLAMTEC LiDAR for mapping and localization, and an IMU for body attitude estimation. ***A. Control Framework Overview*** 

The comprehensive workflow begins with remote control commands transmitted to the motion mode selector and the bio-inspired Central Pattern Generator (CPG) modulation units [5], [34]. The motion mode module derives spatial transformation variables— including multi-variable turning matrices and translation commands—to govern the macro-directional trajectory of the robot chassis [3]. Concurrently, the CPG module generates  periodic  phase  oscillation  variables,  governed  by  the  Hopf  oscillator dynamics, to regulate rhythmic locomotion gait and cycle frequency [34]. 

To facilitate rapid prototyping and ensure modularity, the underlying implementation is developed upon the spider\_bot open-source control framework [33], which provides

[27]；此觀察提供了本研究採用六足簡化設計的依據—— 既能降低結構複雜度、重量與控制頻寬需求，同時保留 蜘蛛敏捷的攀爬特性。受此啟發，本機器人採用六邊形 機身作為核心框架，具備高度結構對稱性與可擴充性， 六隻腿對稱地分布於機身周圍，如圖  1  所示。 雖然六足機器人繼承了蜘蛛的攀爬靈活性，其週期性踏 步運動本質上限制了在平坦開闊地形的平均前進速度。 為解決此效率落差，本研究進一步受水黽（Gerridae）啟 發：水黽以中對腿的快速划槳動作於水面實現高速移 動，Hu  等人  [30]  對其流體動力學機制進行了詳盡分 析，該機制隨後被成功轉移至多足機器人平台  [28]。然 而，真實節肢動物所具備的連續柔性與高自由度，其本 質仰賴靜液壓關節、可變形外骨骼以及高密度神經支配 之肌肉群——這些特性在受限於市售伺服致動器之離散扭

矩、有限軸數與剛性結構材料的實體機器人上難以直接 複製。因此，本設計並未追求完全的仿生複製，而是於 硬體可行範圍內透過機構設計逼近蜘蛛的靜態穩定性與 水黽的連續推進特性：四隻外側腳於末端整合由上方直 流馬達驅動之微型履帶模組，而兩隻中間腳則維持為純 關節式肢體，以保留不規則地形下精準落腳與主動支撐 調整所需的敏捷性。 

本設計的核心創新在於圖  2  所示之非對稱履帶足機構。

1. Hierarchical Mode Selector  階層式模式選擇器  
2. Walking Mode — CPG + Adaptive Impedance Control 行走模式  
2. Tank Mode — Differential PID + IMU  履帶模式

the  foundation  for  the  robot’s  multi-legged  locomotion  and  basic  actuator  ![ref1]communication.  Building  upon  this  framework,  we  bypass  traditional  Inverse  Kinematics (IK) solvers in favor of a dynamics-based approach: the system synthesizes  macroscopic movement directions with multi-phase oscillators to output time-varying  desired  Cartesian  coordinates  P\_d,i  for  each  limb.  To  bridge  operational  space  commands and joint space actuation under irregular topographies, a multi-state control  switching  strategy  is  deployed  based  on  foot-ground  contact  states  and  structural  configurations [6]. This localized reactive behavior model dictates the control paradigm  for each specific limb:  

**Free-Space Regulation (Swing Phase):** In unrestricted free space, the system  employs a trajectory-tracking impedance law. By comparing the desired Cartesian  coordinates with real-time feedback, the controller modulates joint torques to maintain  precise foot-end positioning.  

**Confined-Space Adaptation (Stance Phase):** Upon establishing terrain contact,  the system autonomously shifts to a force-regulated interaction mode. Utilizing real- 

time contact force estimation, an active impedance scheme—inspired by sensorless  contact-adaptation  algorithms  [27]—modulates  operational-space  compliance.  This  approach dynamically adjusts joint torques to attenuate physical impacts and maintain  support forces, effectively decoupling the chassis from terrain-induced disturbances  [27].  Furthermore, a body attitude controller guarantees macro-stabilization during dynamic  locomotion. By fusing real-time feedback of the roll angle φ, pitch angle θ, and center- of-mass (CoM) height—formulated through a continuous-time body state estimation  framework [32]—the attitude stabilizer dynamically computes a virtual compensation  torque τ\_att for each supporting limb. This ensures the main chassis remains isolated  from terrain irregularities, maintaining dynamic balance throughout the motion.  

2. ***Hierarchical Mode Manager  ![ref1]***

The core of the software design lies in the high-level supervisory architecture, which  coordinates  multi-modal  locomotion  to  navigate  hazardous,  non-structured  environments. To govern complex transitions between diverse propulsion mechanisms,  we implement a Finite State Machine (FSM)-based supervisor that integrates predictive  planning and state optimization frameworks tailored for disaster-response scenarios [3].  Aligned with the transformable hybrid platform topology [6], the execution mode M(t)  is  dynamically  determined  via  real-time  feedback  from  the  onboard  Inertial  Measurement Unit (IMU) and exteroceptive height scanning [32]. The state transition  logic is defined by the following decision threshold:  

*M(t) = M\_leg,     if α < α\_thr   and   Δh < h\_thr*  

`        `*M\_track,   if flat open terrain (User Command)*  

`        `*M\_climb,   if α ≥ α\_thr   or   Δh ≥ h\_thr*  

where α denotes the chassis pitch angle and Δh signifies the local terrain elevation  variance. The parameters α\_thr and h\_thr are predefined thresholds triggering non- linear obstacle-overcoming behaviors. When the climbing mode is activated, a hybrid  control  strategy  is  deployed:  the  dual-track  propulsion  is  governed  by  the  FSM  supervisory logic to maintain persistent forward thrust, while the multi-legged linkages  are concurrently driven by a Reinforcement Learning (RL) policy to actively adapt to  irregular  terrain  profiles.  This  hierarchical  supervision  ensures  robust  transition  management, as depicted in the state transition logic illustrated in Fig. 6.

3. ***Legged Mode Movement Control***  

When navigating non-structured or highly irregular terrains, the system switches to the  ![ref1]Legged Locomotion Mode. To absorb physical impacts from uneven ground without  relying  on  external  tactile  force  sensors,  a  dual-mode  foot  motion  framework  is  developed,  combining  a  residual  reinforcement  learning  (RL)  policy  for  terrain  adaptation and a bio-inspired Hopf oscillator network for nominal gait generation.  

1) **Dual-Modal Locomotion Mapping.**   

To balance terrain complexities with physical control constraints, the desired foot tip  trajectory  P\_d,i  is  generated  by  integrating  the  RL-based  residual  policy  with  a  deterministic Hopf-CPG engine.  

**Learning-Based Tactile Adaptive Mode (Residual RL):** Under unpredictable  terrain, a deep RL policy network—trained in NVIDIA Isaac Sim—outputs residual  adjustments to the nominal gait parameters. This policy processes an observation vector  O\_t (base orientation, joint velocities, and estimated foot tip positions) and dynamically  modulates the leg’s rhythmic state to actively adapt to unforeseen terrain profiles.  

**Hopf-CPG  Dynamics  and  Control  Flow:**  To  generate  rhythmically  stable  locomotion, the hexapod system employs a bio-inspired Hopf oscillator network, where  the rhythmic behavior for each leg i is governed by the following differential equations  [37]:  

*ẋ\_i = (μ − x\_i² − y\_i²) x\_i − ω\_i y\_i*  

*ẏ\_i = (μ − x\_i² − y\_i²) y\_i + ω\_i x\_i*  

In this framework, the state variables x\_i and y\_i evolve along a limit cycle with  amplitude μ and intrinsic frequency ω\_i. This dynamics-based approach bridges the  mathematical rhythm and physical actuation through a three-stage integration: first, the  oscillator states are projected into a phase variable φ\_i = atan2(y\_i, x\_i) to index the  Cartesian trajectory P\_d,i(φ\_i); second, the command torque τ\_cmd,i is synthesized via  the  Jacobian-transpose  mapping  and  converted  to  motor  phase  current  I\_cmd,i  =  ![ref1]τ\_cmd,i / k\_t (where k\_t is the torque constant); and finally, the controller leverages the  correlation  between  motor  current  I  and  joint  impedance  as  an  implicit  feedback  mechanism to estimate ground contact states. By treating these fluctuations as intrinsic  feedback,  the  system  autonomously  modulates  the  stance–swing  phase  transition  without relying on external tactile sensors. This integration ensures that the Hopf-CPG  network functions as a robust rhythmic backbone, while the residual RL policy [35],  [36] dynamically adapts the oscillator parameters to compensate for non-structured  terrain perturbations.  

2) **Kinematics-Free Impedance Control Integration.**   

To eliminate the computational burden and singularity issues associated with analytical  Inverse  Kinematics  (IK),  we  implement  a  direct  Jacobian-based  torque  mapping  interface [39]. By leveraging the principle of virtual work, our framework achieves  active  compliance  without  explicit  IK  solvers,  a  paradigm  supported  by  recent  advancements in proprioceptive force-compliance control [38].  

**Residual RL Mapping:** The RL policy generates residual adjustments that modify  the Hopf output, directly mapping to joint-level commands θ\_cmd. To maintain active  compliance, the desired foot tip positions P\_d,i are derived via Forward Kinematics  (FK) based on the link parameters l\_c, l\_f, l\_t.  

**Impedance-to-Torque Mapping:** The system avoids explicit IK by mapping the  task-space impedance law directly to joint torques. Given the virtual force F\_virt,i  defined by the impedance control scheme:  

*F\_virt,i = K\_p (P\_d,i − P\_real,i) + K\_d (Ṗ\_d,i − Ṗ\_real,i)*  

The command joint torque τ\_cmd,i is computed using the Jacobian transpose J\_iᵀ(q),  which relates operational space forces to joint torques through the principle of virtual  

work:  ![ref1]

*τ\_cmd,i = sat( J\_iᵀ(q) F\_virt,i )*  

where J\_iᵀ(q) is computed via the partial derivatives of the kinematics projection. This  direct mapping bypasses the need for IK solvers, enabling the actuators to exhibit  spring-like compliance upon terrain contact. By dynamically adjusting the diagonal  stiffness K\_p and damping K\_d matrices, the controller effectively suppresses terrain- induced impact energy, ensuring chassis stability in challenging environments.  Finally, to guarantee electrical and physical safety of the physical actuators, the actual  command torque τ\_cmd,i sent to the joint motors is bounded via a non-linear saturation  protection operator:  

*τ\_cmd,i = sat(τ\_i, τ\_limit)*  

- *τ\_i,                        if |τ\_i| ≤ τ\_limit*  
  - *τ\_limit · (τ\_i / |τ\_i|),   if |τ\_i| > τ\_limit*  
4. ***Tracked Mode Movement Control***  

When navigating flat, open terrains or executing long-distance high-speed cruising, the  robot switches to the Tracked Propulsion Mode. In this mode, the six-legged linkages  are locked into a predefined, compact home configuration. To mathematically describe  the motion baseline of the dual-track differential drive configuration, let v\_L and v\_R  denote the actual linear velocities of the left and right tracks, respectively. Under  standard differential  kinematics,  the  equivalent  linear  velocity  v\_tank  and  angular  velocity ω\_tank of the robot chassis center are formulated as:  

*v\_tank = (v\_L + v\_R) / 2*  

*ω\_tank = (v\_R − v\_L) / B*  

where B signifies the lateral distance between the left and right tracks. Conversely,  when the user provides teleoperation commands consisting of a target linear velocity v  and a turning angular velocity ω, the nominal reference speed command designated for  ![ref1]pure track cruising (v\_cmd\_tank) is mapped through the inverse kinematics of the  chassis:  

*v\_cmd\_tank = v ± (B · ω) / 2*  

To systematically coordinate multi-source velocity inputs without secondary attitude  compensation loops, a Track Target Velocity Selector is introduced in Level 1. The  finalized reference track velocity command v\_track passed to the actuation interface is  conditionally determined by the supervisory Finite State Machine (FSM):  

*v\_track = v\_cmd\_tank,    if M(t) = M\_track*  

`           `*v\_climb\_assist, if M(t) = M\_climb*  

This  open-loop  feedforward  kinematic  configuration  routes  the  assigned  v\_track  directly to the low-level motor drive firmware (where sprocket wheel radius mapping  ω = v / R is implicitly executed within the Actuation Interface). This strategy ensures a  lightweight control loop highly focused on legged stabilization.  

5. ***RL-Based Climbing Movement Control (Hybrid CPG-RRL Framework)***  

For extreme terrain traversing, the Finite State Machine (FSM) supervisory system  triggers  the  Climbing  Propulsion  Mode.  We  integrate  a  Residual  Reinforcement  Learning (RRL) framework, where the RL policy outputs residuals δP\_RL to refine the  nominal CPG trajectory P\_nom, such that P\_target = P\_nom + δP\_RL. This residual  approach ensures that the fundamental gait stability is preserved by the CPG engine  while the RL agent manages complex terrain adaptations.  

**Policy Architecture and Implementation:** To satisfy the 50 Hz control frequency, the  network  employs  a  [512,  256,  128]  hidden  layer  topology.  We  utilize  the Exponential  Linear  Unit  (ELU)  activation  function  to  ensure  smooth,  continuous gradients, which effectively eliminates high-frequency actuator jitter. The Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm is implemented with a clip\_param of 0.2, serving ![](data:image/png;base64,)as  a safety  boundary  to  prevent  catastrophic  policy updates  during  environmental interaction. 

**Reward  Shaping:**  The  reward  function  R  is  formulated  as  a  multi-objective optimization problem: 

*R = α R\_track + β R\_turn + γ R\_clearance − λ₁ R\_shake − λ₂ R\_osc − λ₃ R\_safety − λ₄ R\_torque* 

where λ₃ R\_safety serves as a critical boundary penalty to force an upright chassis posture, and λ₄ R\_torque incentivizes smooth joint trajectories as evidenced in Fig. 7. 

*[Insert Fig. 7 here]* 

**FIGURE 7.** Reward terms and weight configurations for the learning-based policy. **Decoupled  Propulsion  Mechanism:**  The  track  velocity  v\_track  is  governed deterministically by the FSM to ensure persistent forward thrust, allowing the RRL agent to exclusively coordinate leg linkages. This architectural decoupling significantly compresses the exploration space, facilitating accelerated policy convergence.

1. ***Simulation and Gait Phase Identification*** 

To  validate  the  integration  of  the  Hopf-CPG  network  with  the  active  impedance  ![ref1]controller, the joint torque output of the hexapod system was analyzed during nominal  locomotion. As shown in Fig. 9, the gait exhibits a clear, stable cyclic pattern governed  by the Hopf oscillator dynamics. The rhythmic states x, y—evolving according to ẋ =  (μ − x² − y²) x − ω y and ẏ = (μ − x² − y²) y + ω x—successfully drive the joint-space  actuators through the Jacobian-transpose mapping.  

A distinct torque profile is observed, where the peak torque of approximately 6.0 N·m  corresponds to the stance phase, providing necessary support forces, while the swing  phase maintains a low-torque state of approximately 0.5 N·m. This significant torque  variation confirms the effectiveness of the proposed dynamic model in distinguishing  contact states without relying on external tactile sensors. Furthermore, the convergence  of the torque distribution across all six legs, as illustrated in Fig. 10, demonstrates the  system’s ability to maintain rhythmic consistency and dynamic balance even under  random terrain disturbances. This periodicity validates the stability of our Hopf-CPG  gait generator and the robustness of the impedance-to-torque mapping interface in real- world operating conditions.

2. ***Complex Terrain Motion Experiments***  

To validate the dynamic adaptability of the proposed control strategy, experiments were  conducted on randomly undulating terrains. As shown in Fig. 9 and Fig. 10, the joint  torque output exhibits a clear, stable cyclic pattern, confirming that the Hopf-CPG  engine provides robust rhythmic consistency throughout the locomotion cycle.  

Fig. 11 further demonstrates the system’s response to terrain disturbances, where the  ![ref1]joint torques maintain phase complementarity and periodicity despite the undulating  surface. The experimental results verify two critical capabilities of the framework. First,  the torque mapping interface actively regulates compliance upon foot-terrain contact,  which  effectively  prevents  high-frequency  mechanical  impact  spikes.  Second,  the  quantitative efficiency of this approach is evident as it reduces peak torque transient  spikes by Δτ % compared to traditional non-compliant position control. Ultimately,  these results  demonstrate  that  the controller  successfully  isolates  the chassis  from  terrain-induced disturbances and maintains joint loads within safe operating thresholds,  thereby validating the effectiveness of the dynamics-based torque mapping interface in  hazardous environments.

3. ***Robot Posture and Trajectory Tracking Performance***  

To evaluate the system’s tracking performance and locomotion stability, a straight-line  walking experiment was conducted.  

1) **Trajectory Tracking Analysis:** Fig. 12 demonstrates that the impedance-based  controller successfully enables rhythmic movement of the end-effector. In the X-axis,  the actual trajectory maintains strong phase synchronization with the reference signal,  achieving a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of e\_x mm. In the Z-axis, the consistent  displacement offset observed during the stance phase confirms the system’s active  compliance,  which  effectively  dissipates  ground  reaction  energy.  This  alignment  between the actual output and the Hopf-generated reference validates the efficacy of  our dynamics-based torque mapping approach.  
1) **Body Posture Stability:** To assess locomotion stability, the chassis pitch and roll  

   angles were monitored (Fig. 13). Following an initial t\_w s stabilization phase, the  ![ref1]posture data confirms the following:  

   **Periodic  Response:**  Pitch  and  roll  angles  exhibit  regular  fluctuations  synchronized  with  the  stride  period,  reflecting  the  dynamic  coupling  between  leg  coordination and the Center of Mass (CoM).  

   **Stability Verification:** By applying a detrending process to mitigate cumulative  drift, the fluctuation amplitude is constrained within ±A\_deg°.
